extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, law students, public health advocates, community groups, and organizations who want to submit public comments on federal rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and submitting public comments on federal proposed rules (notice-and-comment rulemaking), including structure, tone, timing, and group organizing tips. Targets both individual commenters and organized/professional submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition & Legal Basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act, federal agencies must consult the public when "making new rules or suggesting changes to current rules." Public comments allow citizens to submit feedback on proposed rule changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the statutory foundation for commenting and frames commenting as the formal mechanism for public input to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing / Comment Periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed rules appear in the Federal Register with comment periods typically lasting 30-60 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit during the published comment period. Agencies must review all substantive comments before finalizing rules; final rules take effect 30 days after publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who Can Participate
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone can submit comments—individuals, students, organizations, and experts alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing: commenting is accessible and "one of the most responsive parts of American democracy," so diverse actors (from lay individuals to organizations) should participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a Public Comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments typically include: 1. Introduction 2. Detailed reaction (sections to keep, remove, or alter with reasoning) 3. Summary/conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this three-part structure to organize points clearly; in the detailed reaction, identify specific provisions and provide reasons for your recommended changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Comments Substantive (identify sections and give reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must review all substantive comments before finalizing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be substantive, explain which sections to keep, remove, or alter and provide reasoning/evidence. Professional submissions should be more evidence-based; individual comments should emphasize personal or community impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone & Focus (individual vs. professional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual comments should be brief, emphasizing personal impact on yourself or community. Professional submissions are more evidence-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone to role: individuals focus on concise, personal narratives; organizations/professionals supply data, citations, and technical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission Method & Confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit through the Federal Register public comment portal linked to the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After submission you'll receive email confirmation viewable on the website within 48 hours — keep confirmation as proof of filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact / Purpose of Commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments "hold federal agencies responsible for the legitimacy of their rules" and reduce future litigation by allowing concerns to be raised before legislation takes effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orient comments toward improving agency decisionmaking and reducing legal vulnerability by pointing out legal, factual, or policy errors during the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosting a Comment Writing Party
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities, community groups, and associations can organize writing parties for law students and public health enthusiasts to gain federal regulation experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided resources include a party checklist, introduction slideshow, and announcement flyer template — use these to train participants and scale submissions while maintaining quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Reference Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Curated list of useful resources for notice-and-comment: Federal Register; Regulations.gov; Public Comment Project; HHS Rulemaking Toolkit; Center for Effective Government guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these sources to find proposed rules, submit via the correct portal, learn best practices for comment content, and consult further toolkits/guidance for technical or legal analysis.
